raw_text:
- The objective of this research is to investigate and explain persistent completion-time differences between sites that ostensibly follow the same nominal work process.
- The scope includes examining measurable factors and observations that distinguish between competing explanations for these differences.

Assumptions
- Site managers report accurate details about their work processes.
- Completion times are a reliable measure of process efficiency.

Research design
- Quasi-experimental design with pre-testing and post-testing to evaluate control and treatment groups.
- Longitudinal study to monitor changes over time, ensuring robustness.

Data or evidence needed
- Performance data with precise timestamps: start and end times for all tasks / processes across the sites.
- Observational data capturing contextual factors such as environment, resource availability, and workflow deviations.
- Self-reported data from site managers about process changes or notable deviations.

Measurement
- Completion time: The time taken from task initiation to task end.
- Work process adherence: Measured through standardized checklists and observed deviations.

Analysis
- Descriptive statistics to summarize initial performance data.
- Statistical analysis to identify correlations between measurable factors and completion times.
- Multivariate regression analysis to determine which factors most significantly predict completion time differences.

Decision / stopping rule
- We will stop the study when we have reached data saturation sufficient to confirm no new significant observations emerge from additional data collection.

Limitations
- Potential self-reporting bias in managers' accounts of process changes.
- External factors not controlled or accounted for in the study design, such as global economic conditions affecting all sites.
- Time constraints limiting data collection periods.
